summary: This part of the Privacy Enhanced Mail series describes three services, key certification, certificate revocation list storage, and revocation list retrieval. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1424 defines email requests for certification authorities to certify a public key, store a certificate revocation list, or return current revocation lists. Replies can be processed as Privacy-Enhanced Mail messages.

subtitle: Email procedures for PEM key certification and certificate revocation lists.

tldr.problem: Privacy-Enhanced Mail needed ways for users to request certification of public keys and to store or retrieve certificate revocation lists.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three services that use email requests and replies: key certification, CRL storage, and CRL retrieval.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1424 is Historic. It is part of the Privacy-Enhanced Mail series and describes services for that framework.

today: RFC 1424 is Historic and has not been obsoleted by a later RFC in the supplied metadata. It is Part IV of the Privacy-Enhanced Mail series, alongside RFC 1421, RFC 1422, and RFC 1423.

sections.title: Three Certification Services
sections.content:
This RFC describes three services for Privacy-Enhanced Mail: key certification, certificate-revocation-list (CRL) storage, and CRL retrieval. Each service uses an email request and reply.

Other services, including certificate revocation and certificate retrieval, are left for certification authorities to define. The authority also chooses where users send requests and may provide non-electronic services outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A user can email a certification authority to request a certificate, submit a revocation list, or retrieve a list. This RFC defines those three request-and-reply services.

sections.title: How the Services Work
sections.content:
For key certification, the requestor sends a self-signed certificate containing a subject name and public key. The authority checks both signatures in the request, creates a certificate, signs it, and returns it with a certification path.

For CRL storage, the authority stores a list only if its signature and certification path are valid. For retrieval, the request names certificate issuers, and the authority returns their latest CRLs.
sections.plainLanguage: The authority verifies a key-certification request before signing a certificate. It checks a submitted revocation list before storing it, and returns current lists for requested issuers.

sections.title: Request and Reply Formats
sections.content:
A certification request is a MIC-ONLY or MIC-CLEAR Privacy-Enhanced Mail message with a self-signed certificate and one signer. The reply uses the same message type and contains the new certificate and its certification path.

CRL storage requests use the CRL message format. CRL retrieval uses a distinct process type, CRL-RETRIEVAL-REQUEST, followed by one or more issuer fields and no encapsulated text.
sections.plainLanguage: Most requests use existing Privacy-Enhanced Mail formats. A CRL retrieval request has its own process type and lists the certificate issuers whose latest lists are requested.

sections.title: Why Certification Requests Are Self-Signed
sections.content:
The requestor's self-signed certificate prevents a request from asking the authority to certify another party's public key. Without this check, a requestor could gain a limited ability to pose as the other party in some signed messages.

The RFC notes that this would not let the requestor decrypt messages intended for that other party.
sections.plainLanguage: The request must prove that the requestor controls the key it wants certified. This prevents a requestor from asking the authority to certify another person's public key.
